'''''Sesbania grandiflora''''', [[common name]]s '''vegetable hummingbird''', '''katurai''', '''agati''', '''agastya''', '''agasya''', '''kathurumurunga''' and '''West Indian pea''', is a [[leguminous]] tree of family [[Fabaceae]] native to [[Malesia]], including [[Malaysia]], [[New Guinea]], and the [[Philippines]].<ref name=POWO/> It is widely distributed globally in [[tropics|equatorial regions]].<ref name=POWO/> The flowers are eaten in [[Southeast Asia|Southeast]] and South Asia.

==Description==
<!-- check Flora of China http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200012311 and use "Cite eFloras" for citation -->

''Sesbania grandiflora'' is a [[leguminous]] tree of family [[Fabaceae]]. It is fast-growing and soft-wooded, and it grows to heights of {{convert|5-20|m|ft|0|abbr=off}}. The [[leaves]] are regular and rounded, and grow to {{convert|15-30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long, with leaflets in 10–20 pairs or more and an odd one. The flowers white, red or pink and are oblong, {{convert|1.5-10|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long in lax, with two to four flower [[raceme]]s. The [[calyx (flower)|calyx]] is campanulate and shallowly two-lipped. These flowers have mild fragrance too. The fruits, or seed pods, look like flat, long, thin green beans. They are slender, falcate or straight, and {{convert|30-45|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long, with a thick suture, and each contains approximately thirty {{convert|8|mm|in|1|abbr=on}} seeds. The tree thrives under full exposure to sunshine and is extremely frost sensitive.

== Distribution and habitat ==
It is native to [[Maritime Southeast Asia]] ([[Malaysia]], [[Indonesia]], [[Philippines]], [[Brunei]]) to New Guinea.<ref name=POWO/> It is cultivated in many parts of [[South India]] and Southeast Asia.<ref name=POWO/> It grows where there is good soil and a hot, humid climate.

==Toxicity==
Feed from the seed can be deadly to chickens.<ref name=heering/>

== Uses ==
[[File:Steamed vegetables CM.jpg|thumb|Steamed flowers (bottom) with other vegetables in a [[Thai cuisine|Thai dish]]]]

''S. grandiflora'' has many traditional uses.<ref>Kirtikar K. R. & B. D. Basu, Indian Medicinal Plants Vol-I, International Book Distributor & Publisher, Dehradun, Edition 2005, bks pp. 735–736</ref> Its flowers are 92% water, 7% [[carbohydrate]]s, 1% [[protein (nutrition)|protein]], and contain no fat.<ref name="fdc">{{cite web |title=Sesbania flower, raw (per 100 g) |url=https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/food-details/168459/nutrients |publisher=FoodData Central, US Department of Agriculture |access-date=14 May 2023 |date=1 April 2019 |archive-date=3 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190403171801/https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/fdc-app.html#/food-details/168459/nutrients |url-status=live }}</ref> In a reference amount of {{convert|100|g}}, the flowers supply 27 [[calorie]]s, and are a rich source of {{Nowrap|[[vitamin C]]}} (88% of the [[Daily Value]], DV) and [[folate]] (26% DV).<ref name=fdc/>

=== Culinary ===
The flowers of ''S. grandiflora'' are eaten as a vegetable in Southeast Asia,<ref name= "Cook's Guide" /> including [[Java]] and [[Lombok]] in Indonesia, the [[Ilocos Region]] of the [[Philippines]], [[Cuisine of Vietnam|Vietnam]], [[Cuisine of Laos|Laos]], and [[Thailand]].{{Citation needed|date=October 2024}} In the [[Thai language]], the flowers are called ดอกแค ''(dok khae)'' and are used in the cuisine both cooked in curries, such as ''[[kaeng som]]'' and ''[[kaeng khae]]'', and raw or blanched with ''[[nam phrik]]''.<ref>[http://thailand.prd.go.th/ebook_bak/story.php?idmag=31&idstory=239 Thailand Illustrated Magazine] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718183710/http://thailand.prd.go.th/ebook_bak/story.php?idmag=31&idstory=239 |date=2011-07-18 }}</ref> The flowers are also prominently used in [[Cambodian cuisine]] and are associated with the [[Bon Om Touk]]. The flower's [[stamen]] is generally discarded before use. In addition to raw and blanched, the flowers can also be battered and [[deep fried]].<ref name= "Cook's Guide" /> In some parts of [[West Bengal]] in India the flowers are locally called Bok ful resembling the [[Egret]] bird from [[Heron]] family of birds. The flowers are a part of the  [[Bengali cuisine]] as they are battered and fried and the fritters are served with meals. In many parts of India the flowers are called Agastya Phool because these flowers bloom in the month of Agastya (August) of [[Sharada (season)|Sharad Ritu]] (Autumn) as per [[Ayurveda]] and is used to prepare [[Pakora]] or dry [[curry]].  

The leaves are also edible.<ref name="Cucio">{{cite book |last1=Cucio |first1=Ardy L. |url=http://bpi.da.gov.ph/bpi/images/Production_guide/pdf/Katuray.pdf |title=Katuray Production Guide |last2=Aragones |first2=Julie Ann A. |publisher=Bureau of Plant Industry, Department of Agriculture, Republic of the Philippines |access-date=9 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191101044427/http://bpi.da.gov.ph/bpi/images/Production_guide/pdf/Katuray.pdf |archive-date=1 November 2019 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The leaves are eaten young. The seed pods are also consumed, similarly only when young.<ref name= "Cook's Guide" >{{cite book |last1=Hutton |first1=Wendy |title=A Cook's Guide to Asian Vegetables |date=2004 |publisher=Periplus Editions |location=Singapore |isbn=0794600786 |pages=22–23}}</ref>

The leaves are sometimes available commercially, but flowers and seed pods come primarily from [[kitchen garden]]s.<ref name= "Cook's Guide" /> The common name of the flower is Heron Flower. It is very popular in Assam, India where it is known as Bok Phool. However, it is not available in abundance in Assam.

Leaves and flowers (particularly of the white-flowered variety) of කතුරු මුරුංගා (''kathurumurunga'') are commonly consumed in Sri Lankan cuisine, where it is cultivated in home gardens.<ref>{{Cite web |date=24 May 2025 |title=HORDI Crop – Kathurumurunga |url=https://doa.gov.lk/hordi-crop-kathurumurunga/ |access-date=24 May 2025 |publisher=Department of Agriculture Sri Lanka}}</ref> The flowers are often stir-fried or batter fried, while the leaves are incorporated into [[Mallung|mallum]], cooked into a curry with coconut milk, or deep-fried.
